statusDescriptions.Aborted_clients: The number of connections that were aborted because the client died without closing the connection properly.
statusDescriptions.Aborted_connects: The number of failed attempts to connect to the MySQL server.
statusDescriptions.Binlog_cache_disk_use: The number of transactions that used the temporary binary log cache but that exceeded the value of binlog_cache_size and used a temporary file to store statements from the transaction.
statusDescriptions.Binlog_cache_use: The number of transactions that used the temporary binary log cache.
statusDescriptions.Connections: The number of connection attempts (successful or not) to the MySQL server.
statusDescriptions.Created_tmp_disk_tables: The number of temporary tables on disk created automatically by the server while executing statements. If Created_tmp_disk_tables is big, you may want to increase the tmp_table_size  value to cause temporary tables to be memory-based instead of disk-based.
statusDescriptions.Created_tmp_files: How many temporary files mysqld has created.
statusDescriptions.Created_tmp_tables: The number of in-memory temporary tables created automatically by the server while executing statements.
statusDescriptions.Delayed_errors: The number of rows written with INSERT DELAYED for which some error occurred (probably duplicate key).
statusDescriptions.Delayed_insert_threads: The number of INSERT DELAYED handler threads in use. Every different table on which one uses INSERT DELAYED gets its own thread.
statusDescriptions.Delayed_writes: The number of INSERT DELAYED rows written.
statusDescriptions.Flush_commands: The number of executed FLUSH statements.
statusDescriptions.Handler_commit: The number of internal COMMIT statements.
statusDescriptions.Handler_delete: The number of times a row was deleted from a table.
statusDescriptions.Handler_discover: The MySQL server can ask the NDB Cluster storage engine if it knows about a table with a given name. This is called discovery. Handler_discover indicates the number of time tables have been discovered.
statusDescriptions.Handler_read_first: The number of times the first entry was read from an index. If this is high, it suggests that the server is doing a lot of full index scans; for example, SELECT col1 FROM foo, assuming that col1 is indexed.
statusDescriptions.Handler_read_key: The number of requests to read a row based on a key. If this is high, it is a good indication that your queries and tables are properly indexed.
statusDescriptions.Handler_read_next: The number of requests to read the next row in key order. This is incremented if you are querying an index column with a range constraint or if you are doing an index scan.
statusDescriptions.Handler_read_prev: The number of requests to read the previous row in key order. This read method is mainly used to optimize ORDER BY … DESC.
statusDescriptions.Handler_read_rnd: The number of requests to read a row based on a fixed position. This is high if you are doing a lot of queries that require sorting of the result. You probably have a lot of queries that require MySQL to scan whole tables or you have joins that don't use keys properly.
statusDescriptions.Handler_read_rnd_next: The number of requests to read the next row in the data file. This is high if you are doing a lot of table scans. Generally this suggests that your tables are not properly indexed or that your queries are not written to take advantage of the indexes you have.
statusDescriptions.Handler_rollback: The number of internal ROLLBACK statements.
statusDescriptions.Handler_update: The number of requests to update a row in a table.
statusDescriptions.Handler_write: The number of requests to insert a row in a table.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_buffer_pool_pages_data: The number of pages containing data (dirty or clean).
statusDescriptions.Innodb_buffer_pool_pages_dirty: The number of pages currently dirty.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_buffer_pool_pages_flushed: The number of buffer pool pages that have been requested to be flushed.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_buffer_pool_pages_latched: The number of latched pages in InnoDB buffer pool. These are pages currently being read or written or that can't be flushed or removed for some other reason.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_buffer_pool_pages_misc: The number of pages busy because they have been allocated for administrative overhead such as row locks or the adaptive hash index. This value can also be calculated as Innodb_buffer_pool_pages_total - Innodb_buffer_pool_pages_free - Innodb_buffer_pool_pages_data.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_buffer_pool_pages_total: Total size of buffer pool, in pages.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_buffer_pool_read_ahead_rnd: The number of "random" read-aheads InnoDB initiated. This happens when a query is to scan a large portion of a table but in random order.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_buffer_pool_read_ahead_seq: The number of sequential read-aheads InnoDB initiated. This happens when InnoDB does a sequential full table scan.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_buffer_pool_read_requests: The number of logical read requests InnoDB has done.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_buffer_pool_reads: The number of logical reads that InnoDB could not satisfy from buffer pool and had to do a single-page read.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_buffer_pool_wait_free: Normally, writes to the InnoDB buffer pool happen in the background. However, if it's necessary to read or create a page and no clean pages are available, it's necessary to wait for pages to be flushed first. This counter counts instances of these waits. If the buffer pool size was set properly, this value should be small.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_buffer_pool_write_requests: The number writes done to the InnoDB buffer pool.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_data_fsyncs: The number of fsync() operations so far.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_data_pending_fsyncs: The current number of pending fsync() operations.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_data_pending_reads: The current number of pending reads.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_data_pending_writes: The current number of pending writes.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_data_read: The amount of data read so far, in bytes.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_data_reads: The total number of data reads.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_data_writes: The total number of data writes.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_data_written: The amount of data written so far, in bytes.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_dblwr_pages_written: The number of pages that have been written for doublewrite operations.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_dblwr_writes: The number of doublewrite operations that have been performed.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_log_waits: The number of waits we had because log buffer was too small and we had to wait for it to be flushed before continuing.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_log_write_requests: The number of log write requests.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_log_writes: The number of physical writes to the log file.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_os_log_fsyncs: The number of fsync() writes done to the log file.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_os_log_pending_fsyncs: The number of pending log file fsyncs.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_os_log_written: The number of bytes written to the log file.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_page_size: The compiled-in InnoDB page size (default 16KB). Many values are counted in pages; the page size allows them to be easily converted to bytes.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_row_lock_current_waits: The number of row locks currently being waited for.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_row_lock_time_avg: The average time to acquire a row lock, in milliseconds.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_row_lock_time: The total time spent in acquiring row locks, in milliseconds.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_row_lock_time_max: The maximum time to acquire a row lock, in milliseconds.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_row_lock_waits: The number of times a row lock had to be waited for.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_rows_deleted: The number of rows deleted from InnoDB tables.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_rows_inserted: The number of rows inserted in InnoDB tables.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_rows_read: The number of rows read from InnoDB tables.
statusDescriptions.Innodb_rows_updated: The number of rows updated in InnoDB tables.
statusDescriptions.Key_blocks_not_flushed: The number of key blocks in the key cache that have changed but haven't yet been flushed to disk. It used to be known as Not_flushed_key_blocks.
statusDescriptions.Key_blocks_unused: The number of unused blocks in the key cache. You can use this value to determine how much of the key cache is in use.
statusDescriptions.Key_blocks_used: The number of used blocks in the key cache. This value is a high-water mark that indicates the maximum number of blocks that have ever been in use at one time.
statusDescriptions.Key_buffer_fraction_%: Percentage of used key cache (calculated value)
statusDescriptions.Key_read_requests: The number of requests to read a key block from the cache.
statusDescriptions.Key_reads: The number of physical reads of a key block from disk. If Key_reads is big, then your key_buffer_size value is probably too small. The cache miss rate can be calculated as Key_reads/Key_read_requests.
statusDescriptions.Key_read_ratio_%: Key cache miss calculated as rate of physical reads compared to read requests (calculated value)
statusDescriptions.Key_write_requests: The number of requests to write a key block to the cache.
statusDescriptions.Key_writes: The number of physical writes of a key block to disk.
statusDescriptions.Key_write_ratio_%: Percentage of physical writes compared to write requests (calculated value)
statusDescriptions.Last_query_cost: The total cost of the last compiled query as computed by the query optimizer. Useful for comparing the cost of different query plans for the same query. The default value of 0 means that no query has been compiled yet.
statusDescriptions.Max_used_connections: The maximum number of connections that have been in use simultaneously since the server started.
statusDescriptions.Not_flushed_delayed_rows: The number of rows waiting to be written in INSERT DELAYED queues.
statusDescriptions.Opened_tables: The number of tables that have been opened. If opened tables is big, your table_open_cache value is probably too small.
statusDescriptions.Open_files: The number of files that are open.
statusDescriptions.Open_streams: The number of streams that are open (used mainly for logging).
statusDescriptions.Open_tables: The number of tables that are open.
statusDescriptions.Qcache_free_blocks: The number of free memory blocks in query cache. High numbers can indicate fragmentation issues, which may be solved by issuing a FLUSH QUERY CACHE statement.
statusDescriptions.Qcache_free_memory: The amount of free memory for query cache.
statusDescriptions.Qcache_inserts: The number of queries added to the cache.
statusDescriptions.Qcache_lowmem_prunes: The number of queries that have been removed from the cache to free up memory for caching new queries. This information can help you tune the query cache size. The query cache uses a least recently used (LRU) strategy to decide which queries to remove from the cache.
statusDescriptions.Qcache_not_cached: The number of non-cached queries (not cachable, or not cached due to the query_cache_type setting).
statusDescriptions.Qcache_queries_in_cache: The number of queries registered in the cache.
statusDescriptions.Qcache_total_blocks: The total number of blocks in the query cache.
statusDescriptions.Rpl_status: The status of failsafe replication (not yet implemented).
statusDescriptions.Select_full_join: The number of joins that do not use indexes. If this value is not 0, you should carefully check the indexes of your tables.
statusDescriptions.Select_full_range_join: The number of joins that used a range search on a reference table.
statusDescriptions.Select_range_check: The number of joins without keys that check for key usage after each row. (If this is not 0, you should carefully check the indexes of your tables.)
statusDescriptions.Select_range: The number of joins that used ranges on the first table. (It's normally not critical even if this is big.)
statusDescriptions.Select_scan: The number of joins that did a full scan of the first table.
statusDescriptions.Slave_open_temp_tables: The number of temporary tables currently open by the replica SQL thread.
statusDescriptions.Slave_retried_transactions: Total (since startup) number of times the replication replica SQL thread has retried transactions.
statusDescriptions.Slave_running: This is ON if this server is a replica that is connected to a primary.
statusDescriptions.Slow_launch_threads: The number of threads that have taken more than slow_launch_time seconds to create.
statusDescriptions.Slow_queries: The number of queries that have taken more than long_query_time seconds.
statusDescriptions.Sort_merge_passes: The number of merge passes the sort algorithm has had to do. If this value is large, you should consider increasing the value of the sort_buffer_size system variable.
statusDescriptions.Sort_range: The number of sorts that were done with ranges.
statusDescriptions.Sort_scan: The number of sorts that were done by scanning the table.
statusDescriptions.Table_locks_immediate: The number of times that a table lock was acquired immediately.
statusDescriptions.Table_locks_waited: The number of times that a table lock could not be acquired immediately and a wait was needed. If this is high, and you have performance problems, you should first optimize your queries, and then either split your table or tables or use replication.
statusDescriptions.Threads_cached: The number of threads in the thread cache. The cache hit rate can be calculated as Threads_created/Connections. If this value is red you should raise your thread_cache_size.
statusDescriptions.Threads_connected: The number of currently open connections.
statusDescriptions.Threads_created: The number of threads created to handle connections. If Threads_created is big, you may want to increase the thread_cache_size value. (Normally this doesn't give a notable performance improvement if you have a good thread implementation.)
statusDescriptions.Threads_running: The number of threads that are not sleeping.

generic.name: Uptime below one day
generic.issue: Uptime is less than 1 day, performance tuning may not be accurate.
generic.recommendation: To have more accurate averages it is recommended to let the server run for longer than a day before running this analyzer
generic.justification: The uptime is only %s

generic.name: Questions below 1,000
generic.issue: Fewer than 1,000 questions have been run against this server. The recommendations may not be accurate.
generic.recommendation: Let the server run for a longer time until it has executed a greater amount of queries.
generic.justification: Current amount of Questions: %s

generic.name: Percentage of slow queries
generic.issue: There is a lot of slow queries compared to the overall amount of Queries.
generic.recommendation: You might want to increase {long_query_time} or optimize the queries listed in the slow query log
generic.justification: The slow query rate should be below 5%%, your value is %s%%.

generic.name: Slow query rate
generic.issue: There is a high percentage of slow queries compared to the server uptime.
generic.recommendation: You might want to increase {long_query_time} or optimize the queries listed in the slow query log
generic.justification: You have a slow query rate of %s per hour, you should have less than 1%% per hour.

generic.name: Long query time
generic.issue: {long_query_time} is set to 10 seconds or more, thus only slow queries that take above 10 seconds are logged.
generic.recommendation: It is suggested to set {long_query_time} to a lower value, depending on your environment. Usually a value of 1-5 seconds is suggested.
generic.justification: long_query_time is currently set to %ds.

generic.name: Slow query logging
generic.issue: The slow query log is disabled.
generic.recommendation: Enable slow query logging by setting {log_slow_queries} to 'ON'. This will help troubleshooting badly performing queries.
generic.justification: log_slow_queries is set to 'OFF'

generic.name: Slow query logging
generic.issue: The slow query log is disabled.
generic.recommendation: Enable slow query logging by setting {slow_query_log} to 'ON'. This will help troubleshooting badly performing queries.
generic.justification: slow_query_log is set to 'OFF'

generic.name: Release Series
generic.issue: The MySQL server version less than 5.1.
generic.recommendation: You should upgrade, as MySQL 5.1 has improved performance, and MySQL 5.5 even more so.
generic.justification: Current version: %s

generic.name: Minor Version
generic.issue: Version less than 5.1.30 (the first GA release of 5.1).
generic.recommendation: You should upgrade, as recent versions of MySQL 5.1 have improved performance and MySQL 5.5 even more so.
generic.justification: Current version: %s

generic.name: Minor Version
generic.issue: Version less than 5.5.8 (the first GA release of 5.5).
generic.recommendation: You should upgrade, to a stable version of MySQL 5.5.
generic.justification: Current version: %s

generic.name: Distribution
generic.issue: Version is compiled from source, not a MySQL official binary.
generic.recommendation: If you did not compile from source, you may be using a package modified by a distribution. The MySQL manual only is accurate for official MySQL binaries, not any package distributions (such as RedHat, Debian/Ubuntu etc).
generic.justification: 'source' found in version_comment

generic.name: Distribution
generic.issue: The MySQL manual only is accurate for official MySQL binaries.
generic.recommendation: Percona documentation is at https://www.percona.com/software/documentation/
generic.justification: 'percona' found in version_comment

generic.name: MySQL Architecture
generic.issue: MySQL is not compiled as a 64-bit package.
generic.recommendation: Your memory capacity is above 3 GiB (assuming the Server is on localhost), so MySQL might not be able to access all of your memory. You might want to consider installing the 64-bit version of MySQL.
generic.justification: Available memory on this host: %s

generic.name: Query caching method
generic.issue: Suboptimal caching method.
generic.recommendation: You are using the MySQL Query cache with a fairly high traffic database. It might be worth considering to use memcached instead of the MySQL Query cache, especially if you have multiple replicas.
generic.justification: The query cache is enabled and the server receives %d queries per second. This rule fires if there is more than 100 queries per second.

generic.id: Percentage of sorts that cause temporary tables
generic.name: Percentage of sorts that cause temporary tables
generic.issue: Too many sorts are causing temporary tables.
generic.recommendation: Consider increasing {sort_buffer_size} and/or {read_rnd_buffer_size}, depending on your system memory limits.
generic.justification: %s%% of all sorts cause temporary tables, this value should be lower than 10%%.

generic.id: Rate of sorts that cause temporary tables
generic.name: Rate of sorts that cause temporary tables
generic.issue: Too many sorts are causing temporary tables.
generic.recommendation: Consider increasing {sort_buffer_size} and/or {read_rnd_buffer_size}, depending on your system memory limits.
generic.justification: Temporary tables average: %s, this value should be less than 1 per hour.

generic.name: Sort rows
generic.issue: There are lots of rows being sorted.
generic.recommendation: While there is nothing wrong with a high amount of row sorting, you might want to make sure that the queries which require a lot of sorting use indexed columns in the ORDER BY clause, as this will result in much faster sorting.
generic.justification: Sorted rows average: %s

generic.name: Rate of joins without indexes
generic.issue: There are too many joins without indexes.
generic.recommendation: This means that joins are doing full table scans. Adding indexes for the columns being used in the join conditions will greatly speed up table joins.
generic.justification: Table joins average: %s, this value should be less than 1 per hour

generic.id: Rate of reading first index entry
generic.name: Rate of reading first index entry
generic.issue: The rate of reading the first index entry is high.
generic.recommendation: This usually indicates frequent full index scans. Full index scans are faster than table scans but require lots of CPU cycles in big tables, if those tables that have or had high volumes of UPDATEs and DELETEs, running 'OPTIMIZE TABLE' might reduce the amount of and/or speed up full index scans. Other than that full index scans can only be reduced by rewriting queries.
generic.justification: Index scans average: %s, this value should be less than 1 per hour

generic.name: Rate of reading fixed position
generic.issue: The rate of reading data from a fixed position is high.
generic.recommendation: This indicates that many queries need to sort results and/or do a full table scan, including join queries that do not use indexes. Add indexes where applicable.
generic.justification: Rate of reading fixed position average: %s, this value should be less than 1 per hour

generic.id: Rate of reading next table row
generic.name: Rate of reading next table row
generic.issue: The rate of reading the next table row is high.
generic.recommendation: This indicates that many queries are doing full table scans. Add indexes where applicable.
generic.justification: Rate of reading next table row: %s, this value should be less than 1 per hour

generic.name: Different tmp_table_size and max_heap_table_size
generic.issue: {tmp_table_size} and {max_heap_table_size} are not the same.
generic.recommendation: If you have deliberately changed one of either: The server uses the lower value of either to determine the maximum size of in-memory tables. So if you wish to increase the in-memory table limit you will have to increase the other value as well.
generic.justification: Current values are tmp_table_size: %s, max_heap_table_size: %s

generic.id: Percentage of temp tables on disk
generic.name: Percentage of temp tables on disk
generic.issue: Many temporary tables are being written to disk instead of being kept in memory.
generic.recommendation: Increasing {max_heap_table_size} and {tmp_table_size} might help. However some temporary tables are always being written to disk, independent of the value of these variables. To eliminate these you will have to rewrite your queries to avoid those conditions (Within a temporary table: Presence of a BLOB or TEXT column or presence of a column bigger than 512 bytes) as mentioned in the beginning of an Article by the Pythian Group
generic.justification: %s%% of all temporary tables are being written to disk, this value should be below 25%%

generic.name: Temp disk rate
generic.issue: Many temporary tables are being written to disk instead of being kept in memory.
generic.recommendation: Increasing {max_heap_table_size} and {tmp_table_size} might help. However some temporary tables are always being written to disk, independent of the value of these variables. To eliminate these you will have to rewrite your queries to avoid those conditions (Within a temporary table: Presence of a BLOB or TEXT column or presence of a column bigger than 512 bytes) as mentioned in the MySQL Documentation
generic.justification: Rate of temporary tables being written to disk: %s, this value should be less than 1 per hour

generic.name: MyISAM key buffer size
generic.issue: Key buffer is not initialized. No MyISAM indexes will be cached.
generic.recommendation: Set {key_buffer_size} depending on the size of your MyISAM indexes. 64M is a good start.
generic.justification: key_buffer_size is 0

generic.id: Max % MyISAM key buffer ever used
generic.name: Max % MyISAM key buffer ever used
generic.issue: MyISAM key buffer (index cache) % used is low.
generic.recommendation: You may need to decrease the size of {key_buffer_size}, re-examine your tables to see if indexes have been removed, or examine queries and expectations about what indexes are being used.
generic.justification: max %% MyISAM key buffer ever used: %s%%, this value should be above 95%%

generic.id: Percentage of MyISAM key buffer used
generic.name: Percentage of MyISAM key buffer used
generic.precondition: key_buffer_size > 0 && !fired('Max % MyISAM key buffer ever used')
generic.issue: MyISAM key buffer (index cache) % used is low.
generic.recommendation: You may need to decrease the size of {key_buffer_size}, re-examine your tables to see if indexes have been removed, or examine queries and expectations about what indexes are being used.
generic.justification: %% MyISAM key buffer used: %s%%, this value should be above 95%%

generic.id: Percentage of index reads from memory
generic.name: Percentage of index reads from memory
generic.issue: The % of indexes that use the MyISAM key buffer is low.
generic.recommendation: You may need to increase {key_buffer_size}.
generic.justification: Index reads from memory: %s%%, this value should be above 95%%

generic.name: Rate of table open
generic.issue: The rate of opening tables is high.
generic.recommendation: Opening tables requires disk I/O which is costly. Increasing {table_open_cache} might avoid this.
generic.justification: Opened table rate: %s, this value should be less than 10 per hour

generic.id: Percentage of used open files limit
generic.name: Percentage of used open files limit
generic.issue: The number of open files is approaching the max number of open files. You may get a "Too many open files" error.
generic.recommendation: Consider increasing {open_files_limit}, and check the error log when restarting after changing {open_files_limit}.
generic.justification: The number of opened files is at %s%% of the limit. It should be below 85%%

generic.name: Rate of open files
generic.issue: The rate of opening files is high.
generic.recommendation: Consider increasing {open_files_limit}, and check the error log when restarting after changing {open_files_limit}.
generic.justification: Opened files rate: %s, this value should be less than 5 per hour

generic.name: Immediate table locks %
generic.issue: Too many table locks were not granted immediately.
generic.recommendation: Optimize queries and/or use InnoDB to reduce lock wait.
generic.justification: Immediate table locks: %s%%, this value should be above 95%%

generic.name: Table lock wait rate
generic.issue: Too many table locks were not granted immediately.
generic.recommendation: Optimize queries and/or use InnoDB to reduce lock wait.
generic.justification: Table lock wait rate: %s, this value should be less than 1 per hour

generic.name: Thread cache
generic.issue: Thread cache is disabled, resulting in more overhead from new connections to MySQL.
generic.recommendation: Enable the thread cache by setting {thread_cache_size} > 0.
generic.justification: The thread cache is set to 0

generic.name: Thread cache hit rate %
generic.issue: Thread cache is not efficient.
generic.recommendation: Increase {thread_cache_size}.
generic.justification: Thread cache hitrate: %s%%, this value should be above 80%%

generic.id: Threads that are slow to launch
generic.name: Threads that are slow to launch
generic.issue: There are too many threads that are slow to launch.
generic.recommendation: This generally happens in case of general system overload as it is pretty simple operations. You might want to monitor your system load carefully.
generic.justification: %s thread(s) took longer than %s seconds to start, it should be 0

generic.name: Slow launch time
generic.issue: Slow_launch_time is above 2s.
generic.recommendation: Set {slow_launch_time} to 1s or 2s to correctly count threads that are slow to launch.
generic.justification: slow_launch_time is set to %s

generic.name: Percentage of used connections
generic.issue: The maximum amount of used connections is getting close to the value of {max_connections}.
generic.recommendation: Increase {max_connections}, or decrease {wait_timeout} so that connections that do not close database handlers properly get killed sooner. Make sure the code closes database handlers properly.
generic.justification: Max_used_connections is at %s%% of max_connections, it should be below 80%%

generic.name: Percentage of aborted connections
generic.issue: Too many connections are aborted.
generic.recommendation: Connections are usually aborted when they cannot be authorized. This article might help you track down the source.
generic.justification: %s%% of all connections are aborted. This value should be below 1%%

generic.name: Rate of aborted connections
generic.issue: Too many connections are aborted.
generic.recommendation: Connections are usually aborted when they cannot be authorized. This article might help you track down the source.
generic.justification: Aborted connections rate is at %s, this value should be less than 1 per hour

generic.name: Percentage of aborted clients
generic.issue: Too many clients are aborted.
generic.recommendation: Clients are usually aborted when they did not close their connection to MySQL properly. This can be due to network issues or code not closing a database handler properly. Check your network and code.
generic.justification: %s%% of all clients are aborted. This value should be below 2%%

generic.name: Rate of aborted clients
generic.issue: Too many clients are aborted.
generic.recommendation: Clients are usually aborted when they did not close their connection to MySQL properly. This can be due to network issues or code not closing a database handler properly. Check your network and code.
generic.justification: Aborted client rate is at %s, this value should be less than 1 per hour

generic.name: Is InnoDB disabled?
generic.issue: You do not have InnoDB enabled.
generic.recommendation: InnoDB is usually the better choice for table engines.
generic.justification: have_innodb is set to 'value'

generic.name: InnoDB log size
generic.issue: The InnoDB log file size is not an appropriate size, in relation to the InnoDB buffer pool.
generic.recommendation: Especially on a system with a lot of writes to InnoDB tables you should set {innodb_log_file_size} to 25% of {innodb_buffer_pool_size}. However the bigger this value, the longer the recovery time will be when database crashes, so this value should not be set much higher than 256 MiB. Please note however that you cannot simply change the value of this variable. You need to shutdown the server, remove the InnoDB log files, set the new value in my.cnf, start the server, then check the error logs if everything went fine. See also this blog entry
generic.justification: Your InnoDB log size is at %s%% in relation to the InnoDB buffer pool size, it should not be below 20%%

generic.name: InnoDB log size
generic.issue: The InnoDB log file size is not an appropriate size, in relation to the InnoDB buffer pool.
generic.recommendation: Especially on a system with a lot of writes to InnoDB tables you should set {innodb_log_file_size} to 25% of {innodb_buffer_pool_size}. However the bigger this value, the longer the recovery time will be when database crashes, so this value should not be set much higher than 256 MiB. Please note however that you cannot simply change the value of this variable. You need to shutdown the server, remove the InnoDB log files, set the new value in my.cnf, start the server, then check the error logs if everything went fine. See also this blog entry
generic.justification: Your InnoDB log size is at %s%% in relation to the InnoDB buffer pool size, it should not be below 20%%

generic.name: Max InnoDB log size
generic.issue: The InnoDB log file size is inadequately large.
generic.recommendation: It is usually sufficient to set {innodb_log_file_size} to 25% of the size of {innodb_buffer_pool_size}. A very big {innodb_log_file_size} slows down the recovery time after a database crash considerably. See also this Article. You need to shutdown the server, remove the InnoDB log files, set the new value in my.cnf, start the server, then check the error logs if everything went fine. See also this blog entry
generic.justification: Your absolute InnoDB log size is %s MiB

generic.name: InnoDB buffer pool size
generic.issue: Your InnoDB buffer pool is fairly small.
generic.recommendation: The InnoDB buffer pool has a profound impact on performance for InnoDB tables. Assign all your remaining memory to this buffer. For database servers that use solely InnoDB as storage engine and have no other services (e.g. a web server) running, you may set this as high as 80% of your available memory. If that is not the case, you need to carefully assess the memory consumption of your other services and non-InnoDB-Tables and set this variable accordingly. If it is set too high, your system will start swapping, which decreases performance significantly. See also this article
generic.justification: You are currently using %s%% of your memory for the InnoDB buffer pool. This rule fires if you are assigning less than 60%%, however this might be perfectly adequate for your system if you don't have much InnoDB tables or other services running on the same machine.

generic.name: MyISAM concurrent inserts
generic.issue: Enable {concurrent_insert} by setting it to 1
generic.recommendation: Setting {concurrent_insert} to 1 reduces contention between readers and writers for a given table. See also MySQL Documentation
generic.justification: concurrent_insert is set to 0

before80003.name: Query cache disabled
before80003.issue: The query cache is not enabled.
before80003.recommendation: The query cache is known to greatly improve performance if configured correctly. Enable it by setting {query_cache_size} to a 2 digit MiB value and setting {query_cache_type} to 'ON'. Note: If you are using memcached, ignore this recommendation.
before80003.justification: query_cache_size is set to 0 or query_cache_type is set to 'OFF'

before80003.name: Query cache efficiency (%)
before80003.issue: Query cache not running efficiently, it has a low hit rate.
before80003.justification: The current query cache hit rate of %s%% is below 20%%

before80003.name: Query Cache usage
before80003.issue: Less than 80% of the query cache is being utilized.
before80003.recommendation: This might be caused by {query_cache_limit} being too low. Flushing the query cache might help as well.
before80003.justification: The current ratio of free query cache memory to total query cache size is %s%%. It should be above 80%%

before80003.name: Query cache fragmentation
before80003.issue: The query cache is considerably fragmented.
before80003.recommendation: Severe fragmentation is likely to (further) increase Qcache_lowmem_prunes. This might be caused by many Query cache low memory prunes due to {query_cache_size} being too small. For a immediate but short lived fix you can flush the query cache (might lock the query cache for a long time). Carefully adjusting {query_cache_min_res_unit} to a lower value might help too, e.g. you can set it to the average size of your queries in the cache using this formula: (query_cache_size - qcache_free_memory) / qcache_queries_in_cache
before80003.justification: The cache is currently fragmented by %s%% , with 100%% fragmentation meaning that the query cache is an alternating pattern of free and used blocks. This value should be below 20%%.

before80003.name: Query cache low memory prunes
before80003.issue: Cached queries are removed due to low query cache memory from the query cache.
before80003.recommendation: You might want to increase {query_cache_size}, however keep in mind that the overhead of maintaining the cache is likely to increase with its size, so do this in small increments and monitor the results.
before80003.justification: The ratio of removed queries to inserted queries is %s%%. The lower this value is, the better (This rules firing limit: 0.1%%)

before80003.name: Query cache max size
before80003.issue: The query cache size is above 128 MiB. Big query caches may cause significant overhead that is required to maintain the cache.
before80003.recommendation: Depending on your environment, it might be performance increasing to reduce this value.

before80003.name: Query cache min result size
before80003.issue: The max size of the result set in the query cache is the default of 1 MiB.
before80003.recommendation: Changing {query_cache_limit} (usually by increasing) may increase efficiency. This variable determines the maximum size a query result may have to be inserted into the query cache. If there are many query results above 1 MiB that are well cacheable (many reads, little writes) then increasing {query_cache_limit} will increase efficiency. Whereas in the case of many query results being above 1 MiB that are not very well cacheable (often invalidated due to table updates) increasing {query_cache_limit} might reduce efficiency.

innodb_data_home_dir.title: Data home directory
innodb_data_home_dir.desc: The common part of the directory path for all InnoDB data files.

innodb_autoextend_increment.title: Autoextend increment
innodb_autoextend_increment.desc: The increment size for extending the size of an autoextending tablespace when it becomes full.

innodb_buffer_pool_size.title: Buffer pool size
innodb_buffer_pool_size.desc: The size of the memory buffer InnoDB uses to cache data and indexes of its tables.

innodb_data_home_dir.title: Data home directory
innodb_data_home_dir.desc: The common part of the directory path for all InnoDB data files.

innodb_autoextend_increment.title: Autoextend increment
innodb_autoextend_increment.desc: The increment size for extending the size of an autoextending tablespace when it becomes full.

innodb_buffer_pool_size.title: Buffer pool size
innodb_buffer_pool_size.desc: The size of the memory buffer InnoDB uses to cache data and indexes of its tables.

myisam_data_pointer_size.title: Data pointer size
myisam_data_pointer_size.desc: The default pointer size in bytes, to be used by CREATE TABLE for MyISAM tables when no MAX_ROWS option is specified.

myisam_recover_options.title: Automatic recovery mode
myisam_recover_options.desc: The mode for automatic recovery of crashed MyISAM tables, as set via the --myisam-recover server startup option.

myisam_max_sort_file_size.title: Maximum size for temporary sort files
myisam_max_sort_file_size.desc: The maximum size of the temporary file MySQL is allowed to use while re-creating a MyISAM index (during REPAIR TABLE, ALTER TABLE, or LOAD DATA INFILE).

myisam_max_extra_sort_file_size.title: Maximum size for temporary files on index creation
myisam_max_extra_sort_file_size.desc: If the temporary file used for fast MyISAM index creation would be larger than using the key cache by the amount specified here, prefer the key cache method.

myisam_repair_threads.title: Repair threads
myisam_repair_threads.desc: If this value is greater than 1, MyISAM table indexes are created in parallel (each index in its own thread) during the repair by sorting process.

myisam_sort_buffer_size.title: Sort buffer size
myisam_sort_buffer_size.desc: The buffer that is allocated when sorting MyISAM indexes during a REPAIR TABLE or when creating indexes with CREATE INDEX or ALTER TABLE.

pbxt_index_cache_size.title: Index cache size
pbxt_index_cache_size.desc: This is the amount of memory allocated to the index cache. Default value is 32MB. The memory allocated here is used only for caching index pages.

pbxt_record_cache_size.title: Record cache size
pbxt_record_cache_size.desc: This is the amount of memory allocated to the record cache used to cache table data. The default value is 32MB. This memory is used to cache changes to the handle data (.xtd) and row pointer (.xtr) files.

pbxt_log_cache_size.title: Log cache size
pbxt_log_cache_size.desc: The amount of memory allocated to the transaction log cache used to cache on transaction log data. The default is 16MB.

pbxt_log_file_threshold.title: Log file threshold
pbxt_log_file_threshold.desc: The size of a transaction log before rollover, and a new log is created. The default value is 16MB.

pbxt_transaction_buffer_size.title: Transaction buffer size
pbxt_transaction_buffer_size.desc: The size of the global transaction log buffer (the engine allocates 2 buffers of this size). The default is 1MB.

pbxt_checkpoint_frequency.title: Checkpoint frequency
pbxt_checkpoint_frequency.desc: The amount of data written to the transaction log before a checkpoint is performed. The default value is 24MB.

pbxt_data_log_threshold.title: Data log threshold
pbxt_data_log_threshold.desc: The maximum size of a data log file. The default value is 64MB. PBXT can create a maximum of 32000 data logs, which are used by all tables. So the value of this variable can be increased to increase the total amount of data that can be stored in the database.

pbxt_garbage_threshold.title: Garbage threshold
pbxt_garbage_threshold.desc: The percentage of garbage in a data log file before it is compacted. This is a value between 1 and 99. The default is 50.

pbxt_log_buffer_size.title: Log buffer size
pbxt_log_buffer_size.desc: The size of the buffer used when writing a data log. The default is 256MB. The engine allocates one buffer per thread, but only if the thread is required to write a data log.

pbxt_data_file_grow_size.title: Data file grow size
pbxt_data_file_grow_size.desc: The grow size of the handle data (.xtd) files.

pbxt_row_file_grow_size.title: Row file grow size
pbxt_row_file_grow_size.desc: The grow size of the row pointer (.xtr) files.

pbxt_log_file_count.title: Log file count
pbxt_log_file_count.desc: This is the number of transaction log files (pbxt/system/xlog*.xt) the system will maintain. If the number of logs exceeds this value then old logs will be deleted, otherwise they are renamed and given the next highest number.
